strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated framework: composing Tweedie-denoised means with a unit-sum (corrector) or zero-sum (resampler) weight constraint, with a simple lemma showing why this preserves the CFG form where naive score composition (Liu et al., 2022) does not. This gives a clean unifying lens on existing correction-based and composable approaches.

The method is genuinely gradient-free and model-agnostic, avoiding backpropagation through the denoiser, and this is demonstrated on a second architecture (PixArt-Σ), which is more than many comparable works do.

Evaluation includes a reasonable set of baselines (Attend-and-Excite, SynGen, Divide-and-Bind, ToMe, InitNO, Composable Diffusion), an ablation decomposing resampling, correction, and weight modulation (Table 2), a time-complexity comparison (Table 3), and fairly extensive hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix, including honest failure cases (Fig. 7).
The characterization of when resampling vs. correction is effective across timesteps (Fig. 2) is a useful empirical contribution that motivates the hybrid schedule.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the weighted Tweedie-mean composition for multi-concept generation is very close to TweedieMix (Kwon & Ye, 2025), and the contrastive corrector p(x|C)/∏p(x|ci)^wk is essentially the negation/marginal-composition idea studied in energy-based compositional diffusion (Du et al., 2024) and ConFORM (Meral et al., 2024). The paper acknowledges the connections but the delta—a weight constraint plus closeness-aware modulation—is incremental, and the negative weights are akin to negative prompting.

The link between the corrector distribution (Eq. 12) and the practical algorithm (Eq. 13) is not formally established: linearly averaging Tweedie means is not equivalent to sampling from the ratio distribution p(x|C)/∏p(x|ci)^wk, and no sampling-theoretic argument (e.g., MCMC, SMC) is given. As a result, the claimed 'empirical validation of the hypothesis on mode overlap' is an overreach—the metrics only show better prompt adherence, not that mode overlap is the cause or that sampling from the corrector distribution occurs.
The theoretical contributions (Lemmas 1–3) are elementary algebra on the linearity of the CFG function; they are clearly written but too thin to constitute a substantive theoretical contribution.

Evaluation is narrow: only the Chefer et al. benchmark with two automatic metrics (BLIP-VQA, ImageReward). No human evaluation, no T2I-CompBench despite citing it, no statistical significance or variance across seeds, and only ~2 prompts shown per figure qualitatively. On the Objects category CO3 actually underperforms ToMe on BLIP-VQA (0.5146 vs. 0.6440), and the paper's explanation (concept parsing strips adjectives, so color attributes are not separately guided) reveals a notable design limitation for attribute binding.

Inconsistent hyperparameter reporting undermines reproducibility: the main implementation states guidance λ = 5.0, while all ablations use λ = 0.8–0.9; Fig. 2's setup is unspecified; there are typos and unfinished sentences ('an well-known approach', 'Ablations Studies are preformed', 'Our intuitive idea is to go away from problematic modes').

Efficiency claim is overstated: at 19.9s per sample vs. 7.2s for base SDXL (~2.8x slower), CO3 is the most expensive sampling-based method in Table 3, which sits uneasily with the 'lightweight' framing and weakens the practical case against optimization-based methods that it outperforms only modestly.

strengths: The proposed method is practical: plug-and-play, gradient-free, and model-agnostic, and it is evaluated on two backbone models (SDXL and PixArt-Σ), which partially supports the model-agnostic claim.

The paper makes a genuine attempt to unify prior correction-based and compositional approaches under a Tweedie-mean composition view, and provides simple lemmas (Lemma 2, Lemma 3) clarifying when the composed noise preserves the CFG functional form.

The evaluation includes a reasonable set of baselines (Attend-and-Excite, SynGen, Divide-and-Bind, ToMe, InitNO, Composable Diffusion), an ablation table decomposing the components (resampling, corrector, weight modulation), and a hyperparameter sweep in the appendix.
The paper includes efficiency analysis (Table 3), failure case visualization (Fig. 7), and a reproducibility statement, which is better practice than many similar submissions.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core method is a linear combination of Tweedie means with negative weights on concept conditions. This is very close to existing work — the paper itself acknowledges that Kwon & Ye (2025) 'TweedieMix' uses a similar composition, and Composable Diffusion (Liu et al., 2022) composes conditional scores. The delta boils down to composing in Tweedie-denoised space rather than noise space plus a heuristic weight modulation, which is an incremental contribution.

The theoretical analysis is thin. Lemma 2 and 3 are elementary algebraic manipulations (weights must sum to 1 for a CFG-form composition), which do not constitute a meaningful theoretical contribution. More importantly, the central technical gap is unaddressed: the paper motivates sampling from the corrector distribution p̃t(xt|C) ∝ pt(xt|C)/∏pt(xt|ck) (Eq. 12), but never establishes that linearly composing Tweedie means (Eq. 13) actually samples from, or even approximates, this distribution. The connection between the hypothesis and the algorithm is asserted rather than derived.

The empirical validation of the central hypothesis (mode overlap between p(x|C) and p(x|ci)) is indirect at best. The evidence is that ImageReward/BLIP-VQA scores improve; there is no direct measurement of mode overlap, no diagnostic analysis, and no comparison against alternative explanations for the observed gains.

The internal logic is inconsistent: the resampler (sum of weights = 0) is admitted to be 'theoretically valid only at t = T', yet it is applied at t < T because it 'practically' helps. This undercuts the paper's own theoretical framing of valid Tweedie-mean composition.

Evaluation has notable gaps. Only the (limited) Chefer et al. prompt benchmark is used quantitatively; the widely used T2I-CompBench (cited by the authors) is not evaluated. BLIP-VQA gains on the Objects category are marginal (0.5146 vs. 0.4926 for base SDXL and well behind ToMe at 0.6440). There is no human evaluation, no CLIP-based metric, no statistical significance testing, and no variance across seeds despite the method being heavily sampling-dependent.

Compute cost is downplayed: CO3 costs 19.9s per image vs. 7.2s for base SDXL (~3x), and it requires extra forward passes per concept per iteration (P=5 iterations). This is not clearly accounted for when claiming advantages over optimization-based baselines.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters is significant: Table 4-8 show noticeable performance swings with β, num_ts, num_steps, and λ, and some ablation settings even regress below the base model. The method's robustness is thus questionable, yet the main results use a single tuned configuration.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: multiple typos and inconsistencies ('an well-known approach', 'Ablations Studies are preformed', 'conretize', inconsistent naming of InitNO/InitNo, 'taihang Hu' lowercased, stray punctuation in the abstract), an unlabeled/unclear Figure 2, and Eq. 20-21 formatting issues in the appendix. These issues, while individually minor, collectively suggest insufficient polish.

The 'if and only if' claim in Lemma 1a conflates 'can be written in Tweedie-mean form' with 'is a valid Tweedie mean of a meaningful distribution'; the composed noise ε̃ corresponds to no actual concept distribution in general, so the theoretical interpretation is weaker than presented.

strengths: The proposed method is genuinely plug-and-play, gradient-free, and model-agnostic, which is a practical advantage over attention/gradient-based correction methods that require architectural access.

The framing in Tweedie-mean space is clean, and Lemma 1/2 provide a simple but useful characterization: unit-sum weights preserve the CFG form while zero-sum weights act as pure noise resampling. This gives a coherent explanation for why Composable Diffusion's arbitrary weight composition can produce off-manifold samples.

Comprehensive empirical work: comparison against a broad set of recent baselines (Attend-and-Excite, SynGen, Divide-and-Bind, ToMe, InitNO, Composable Diffusion), a component-wise ablation (Table 2), hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix, an efficiency comparison (Table 3), and generalization to PixArt-Σ.
Honest treatment of limitations: dedicated failure-case analysis (Fig. 7, A.6.1) and a reproducibility statement with hyperparameters and implementation details (Stanza parsing, Tc, Tr, P, β).
weaknesses: There is a gap between the claimed theory and the actual method. The paper motivates sampling from p̃(x|C) ∝ p(x|C)/∏p(x|ci) (Eq. 1), but never derives that linearly composing Tweedie means (Eq. 13) corresponds to sampling from this corrector distribution. Since the Tweedie mean is nonlinear in the score, score-space composition arguments do not carry over to Tweedie-mean space; the connection is asserted rather than proven. The lemmas only show algebraic consistency with the CFG form, not validity of the corrective distribution.

The central hypothesis (problematic modes arise from overlap with individual-concept modes, Fig. 1) is supported only by a toy 2D illustration. The claim that the empirical gains 'validate' the hypothesis is overclaimed; no direct measurement of mode overlap or analysis of the score landscape is provided.

The theoretical contribution is modest: Lemma 2 is elementary algebra on an affine combination. Overall the paper reads as a well-engineered heuristic (unit-sum vs. zero-sum weights, closeness-aware modulation with a hand-set β, anchor w0 = 1.0 vs 2.0, thresholds Tc/Tr) rather than a principled sampler, and the relationship to the concurrent TweedieMix (Kwon & Ye, 2025) is not clearly delineated beyond the resampler/corrector framing.

Evaluation is limited: only two automated metrics (BLIP-VQA, ImageReward), no human evaluation, no variance over seeds or confidence intervals, and the main benchmark contains only two-concept prompts of restricted forms. Results are mixed in places (e.g., the Objects category, where ToMe clearly outperforms CO3 on BLIP-VQA), which is acknowledged only briefly.
The benchmark mixes SD1.5-based and SDXL-based baselines in a single table, complicating attribution; only a subset of baselines was adapted to SDXL.
Efficiency cost is roughly 2.8× that of the base model (19.9s vs 7.2s per sample), which somewhat undercuts the 'lightweight corrective guidance' claim and deserves discussion in the main text.

Hyperparameters are numerous and somewhat fragile: the appendix sweeps show performance is sensitive to β, λ, num_ts, num_steps, and num_resampling, and the best values (e.g., num_ts=10 in Table 5, contradicting the saturation claim around 0.75T in Fig. 2) are not fully consistent with the main-text narrative.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-known and practically important failure mode of text-to-image diffusion models (concept suppression/collision in multi-concept prompts) with a plug-and-play, gradient-free, model-agnostic correction that requires no retraining — a practically attractive operating point.

The Tweedie-mean composition framing is cleanly worked out: Lemma 1 and Proposition 1 clarify why score compositions with arbitrary weights (e.g., Composable Diffusion) do not correspond to a valid CFG-form noise, and characterize the unit-sum (corrector) and zero-sum (resampler) regimes.

The hybrid resampler/corrector design is empirically motivated (Figure 2 characterization across timesteps) and the Closeness-Aware weight modulation gives an adaptive mechanism to repel from concept-dominated modes.

Evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: SDXL and PixArt-Σ backbones, three benchmarks (Attend-Excite, T2ICompbench Complex, RareBench), multiple metrics (BLIP-VQA, ImageReward, DINOv2), a human evaluation with 11 participants, strong baseline coverage spanning optimization-based, composable, and LLM-augmented methods, component ablations, extensive hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix, solver/step-budget generalization (DPM++, low-step regimes), and runtime/memory analysis.
Reproducibility is well supported: implementation details, concept extraction procedure (Stanza parsing), baseline adaptation notes, code availability, and failure-case analysis are provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin: Lemma 1 is essentially trivial linear algebra (preservation of the affine CFG form under unit-sum weights), and the paper's actual sampling procedure (weighted Tweedie-mean composition in Algorithm 3, plus mean normalization and unconditioned manifold correction) is never rigorously connected to the claimed corrector distribution p̃t ∝ pt(xt|C)/∏pt(xt|ck)^wk. No derivation shows the implemented update samples from (or approximates) Eq. 12, so the probabilistic justification remains heuristic.

The central hypothesis — that failures arise from overlap between joint modes p(x|C) and individual concept modes p(x|ci) — is informal and only indirectly supported by aggregate metric improvements; there is no direct diagnostic evidence (e.g., measuring mode overlap, distributional analysis, or probing p(x|C)/p(x|ci)) validating the mechanism.

Incremental novelty relative to prior work: the resampler is acknowledged to be similar to TweedieMix's composition, and the corrector is a negative-weight variant of score composition; the delta over existing compositional methods is primarily a weight-constraint observation plus scheduling and modulation heuristics.

Some results are mixed or modest: CO3 does not dominate on all categories (e.g., loses to baselines on some O-O/DINOv2 entries and RareBench human evaluation vs. SDXL), and the improvement margins on ImageReward/BLIP-VQA — both known to be imperfect proxies — are not always large.

Computational overhead is notable: ~2.8x the wall-clock of base SDXL (19.9s vs 7.2s at 50 steps) due to multiple forward passes per corrected step and corrector iterations, which weakens the 'lightweight' claim; the trade-off versus cheaper gradient-based baselines deserves more analysis.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is a concern: main text reports λ=5.0 while appendix sweeps use λ=0.8–0.9, and performance varies noticeably across β, num_ts, and num_steps; guidance on how to set these for new models/prompts is limited, and the human evaluation cohort (11 participants) is small.
Writing has minor issues (e.g., unnumbered highlight legend in Table 1, garbled citations like 'taihang Hu', several typos) that slightly detract from polish.

strengths: The paper is technically sound in its core analysis: Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 give a clean characterization of when linear composition of Tweedie means / CFG noises yields a valid Tweedie-mean update (sum of weights = 1) versus when it degenerates, and this cleanly explains why composable-diffusion-style score mixing with arbitrary weights can produce off-manifold samples.

The method is fully gradient-free and model-agnostic (demonstrated on both SDXL and PixArt-Σ), which distinguishes it from attention/gradient-based correction baselines and makes it practically attractive; runtime/memory analysis shows reasonable overhead.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: Attend-Excite benchmarks, T2ICompbench Complex, RareBench subsets, human evaluation with 11 participants, ablations of all major components (resampling, corrector, weight modulation), hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix, and tests under DPM++/low-step regimes.
Ablation results (Table 3) show that each component contributes, and the hybrid resampler→corrector schedule is empirically motivated by the timestep analysis in Figure 2.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: the 'resampler' is essentially the multi-concept composition of Tweediemix (Kwon & Ye, 2025) reused as an initial-noise sampler (the authors even compare against Tweediemix in Table 1), and the 'corrector' is a weighted negative composition close in spirit to composable diffusion. The delta reduces to the unit-sum weight constraint, the closeness-aware weight modulation, and the hybrid schedule — incremental contributions presented as a new framework.

The central hypothesis (misalignment arises from 'mode collisions' between joint and individual concept distributions) is never directly validated. Improvements on ImageReward/BLIP-VQA are offered as 'empirical evidence of our hypothesis', but these are coarse text-image alignment metrics that cannot distinguish mode-overlap from many other failure mechanisms; no diagnostic experiments probe the hypothesis itself.

Evaluation inconsistencies and over-claiming: Table 2 shows CO3 is clearly worse than SDXL on the RareBench 'Relations' category (0.2588 vs 0.3607 IR), yet the text claims it 'consistently outperforms or matches the best-performing baselines across all categories and metrics'. Similarly, Object-Object BLIP-VQA in Table 1 is below several baselines. Human evaluation is small (11 participants) with no significance testing.

Metric concerns: ImageReward is a learned preference model susceptible to bias and to being gamed by stylization effects; some qualitative results (e.g., Figure 9, stylized/low-detail backgrounds acknowledged in Appendix A.6) suggest the method trades background richness for concept obedience, which the automatic metrics may not penalize adequately.

Unclear/inconsistent methodological details: the main text states guidance scale λ = 5.0 for experiments, while all appendix ablations use λ ∈ {0.8, 0.9} with no reconciliation; the theoretical justification for applying the 'resampler' (valid only at t = T per Proposition 1b) at t > 0.9T is hand-waved as empirically beneficial; the relationship between p̃ in Eq. 12 and the actual Tweedie-mean composition in Eq. 13 is loose (composing means is not sampling from the quotient distribution in general).

Writing and presentation issues reduce confidence: several typos in tables (e.g., '0.48666', '0.53666', '0.61166' in Table 2), an incomplete code URL in the abstract, and repetitive prose across Sections 1, 3 and 6.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: multi-concept prompt fidelity in T2I diffusion is an active and important area, and the 'mode overlap' hypothesis provides an intuitive framing for concept suppression.

The method is genuinely gradient-free, model-agnostic, and plug-and-play, which is a practical advantage over the majority of attention/gradient-based correction baselines (Attend-Excite, SynGen, Divide-Bind, InitNO), and the paper is transparent about this distinction (Table 1 'Properties' columns).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three benchmark suites (Attend-Excite, T2ICompbench, RareBench), a broad set of 10+ baselines including recent SOTA (ToMe, TweedieMix, R2F, Magnet), multiple metrics (BLIP-VQA, ImageReward, DINOv2), plus human evaluation following the R2F protocol.

Good ablation studies (Table 3, Figure 5) that decompose the contribution of resampling, corrector, and weight modulation, as well as extensive hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix (Tables 9-13) and generalization to another base model (PixArt-Σ, Table 4) and to other solvers / low-step regimes (Tables 6-7).

The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1, Lemma 1) is correct and gives a clean explanation for why unit-sum weights preserve the CFG form, offering a plausible account of why composable-diffusion heuristics produce off-manifold samples.

Honest reporting of limitations: failure cases (Fig. 8), concept-obedience behavior regarding backgrounds (A.6), and runtime/memory costs (Table 8). Reproducibility statement and implementation details are provided.
weaknesses: The link between the proposed corrector distribution (Eq. 12, a ratio of densities) and the actual sampling procedure (weighted composition of Tweedie means, Eq. 13) is informal. No derivation shows that weighted Tweedie-mean composition actually samples from (or approximates) p(x|C)/∏p(x|ci); the theoretical results only characterize when the composed mean is a 'valid' Tweedie mean, not what distribution it targets. The central hypothesis about mode overlap remains plausible but empirically indirect.

Novelty is moderate: the core operation is a linear recombination of Tweedie means / noise predictions, closely related to Composable Diffusion (Liu et al., 2022) and TweedieMix (Kwon & Ye, 2025); the main new ingredients are the negative/unit-sum weighting constraint and the closeness-aware modulation heuristic, which are relatively incremental.

Inconsistencies in reported settings undermine confidence: the main text states guidance λ = 5.0 and β = 0.8, while appendix sweeps use λ ∈ {0.8, 0.9} and β up to 1.1 with different best values (e.g., num_resampling=3 vs. main text 'first three steps'), and SDXL baseline numbers differ between Table 3 and Tables 6-8. These should be reconciled.

Efficiency claims are overstated: 'lightweight' CO3 takes ~19.9s per image vs. 7.2s for base SDXL (Table 8), a ~2.8x slowdown from K+1 forward passes per corrected step; this cost is disclosed but sits uneasily with the plug-and-play framing.

Human evaluation uses only 11 participants, and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for any quantitative comparison; several per-category results are mixed (e.g., CO3 underperforms baselines on the RareBench 'Relations' ImageReward in Table 2), which weakens the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

Comparison fairness concerns: several baselines in Table 1 were designed for SD1.5 while CO3 uses SDXL, and TweedieMix is evaluated without its fine-tuned customization stage; differences in base model capability confound some comparisons.

Writing/polish issues: lowercase citation names ('taihang Hu'), a 'Code is available at' sentence with a missing URL, and some typos ('resulated', 'conretize'); these suggest the manuscript was not fully proofread.
